studies.significance: The RT read is geometry plus fractionation: a custom PMMA mold held dose at 5 mm depth within 5% of prescription over curved facial surfaces, with 180 cGy fractions to 6000-6500 cGy and no severe late effects. Whether that conformality keeps its late-toxicity profile with fewer, larger fractions was not tested here.
studies.monday_clinic: In node-negative BCC/SCC on curved facial skin (nose, eyelid, ear) where an electron or orthovoltage field fits poorly, this supports HDR surface-mold brachytherapy as a conformal RT option; it does not inform hypofractionated mold schedules or deeply invasive lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Prospective single-institution series**, 136 consecutive pts treated 1992-1997 in Barcelona. **Minimum follow-up 12 mo**; median follow-up not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pathologically confirmed **facial BCC (102) or SCC (34)**, **73 primary and 63 recurrent** after prior local therapy. Gross tumor left in place in most; margins positive in 128. No nodal or distant disease on CT head/neck and chest X-ray.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: HDR Ir-192 via **117 custom PMMA molds** (3-7 parallel catheters, 5 mm bolus layer) or 19 Brock applicators. **6000-6500 cGy in 33-36 fx of 180 cGy** at 5 mm depth; lesions ≥4 cm boosted **1800 cGy/10 fx** after a 3-wk rest to 7500-8000 cGy. Eye shielded with a 5 mm lead sheet in the mold.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: All pts complete responders; **3 local recurrences** (1/73 primary, 2/63 recurrent). **5y actuarial LC 98%** overall, **99% primary**, **87% recurrent**; no regional or distant failure.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Erythema G1 in 117 and G2 in 19; 14 (10%) had G1 ulceration at 6 wk, all healed by 4 mo. Good/excellent cosmesis **98% at 6 mo**; **no severe late complications**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Primary-tumor LC of **99%** sits alongside the **95%** superficial X-ray result in the Lovett EBRT series and above Lovett's **77%** with electrons. Daly's Ir-192 interstitial implants reached **96%** LC but with **18%** severe late effects, the toxicity gap the mold approach is designed to close.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents node-negative facial BCC/SCC, including lesions on curved surfaces and post-surgical recurrences. Does not represent hypofractionated HDR schedules, nodal disease, or high-risk SCC defined by depth of invasion (not measured).

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Dose per fraction (180 cGy) far from modern short-course skin brachy, so the late-effect profile may not transfer. Recurrent-tumor LC timepoint reported inconsistently (5y vs 4y), and cosmesis was graded by the treating team.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The contribution is technical: a reproducible, afterloaded surface applicator that conforms to non-flat facial anatomy with a sharp edge gradient. It shows high control with conventional fractionation but does not settle how it compares head-to-head with superficial X-ray, electrons, or Mohs.

studies.interpretation:
This is a technique paper wearing the clothes of an outcomes paper, and it should be read that way. The clinically interesting claim is not that radiotherapy controls facial basal and squamous cell carcinoma; that was established long before this series. The claim is that a custom-built acrylic mold, carrying afterloading catheters over an impression of the patient's own face, can deliver a homogeneous dose at 5 mm depth across curved anatomy (nose, eyelid, ear, preauricular skin) with a sharp falloff at the applicator edge. The dosimetric evidence for that claim is direct and checkable: variation at depth within 5% of prescription, and thermoluminescent readings that matched the plan within 5%. That is the part of the paper most likely to transfer.

The control figures, 99% at five years for primaries and 87% for recurrences, look excellent, but their footing is softer than they appear. The cohort is single-institution, without a comparator, and follow-up is described only by a 12-month minimum; the at-risk counts at five years are a minority of the starting cohort. The recurrent-tumor control rate is attributed to five years in the Results and four years in the Discussion, and the reported lesion size distribution is internally inconsistent. None of this makes the result wrong, but it means the headline numbers should be held loosely and the comparisons to other series even more loosely.

The comparisons the authors draw are to Lovett's external-beam series, where superficial X-rays reached 95% and electrons only 77%, and to Daly's interstitial iridium implants, which matched on control at 96% but at the cost of 18% severe late effects. The more defensible reading is that the mold approach plausibly combines implant-level conformality with the noninvasive, low-toxicity profile of superficial X-rays, especially on surfaces where an electron or orthovoltage field cannot sit flat. The cross-series comparison cannot prove superiority: different eras, different case mixes, and different definitions of control.

The fractionation is the biggest barrier to transfer. Thirty-three to thirty-six fractions of 180 cGy, plus a boost after a three-week break for larger lesions, is a seven-week-plus commitment for a population whose mean age was 67. The authors attribute the absence of severe late complications to the small fraction size, contrasting it with the 300 to 400 cGy fractions in Lovett's series. That explanation is reasonable but untested here, and it cuts against the direction contemporary skin brachytherapy has taken toward short courses. A reader should not assume the late-cosmesis profile carries over to hypofractionated mold treatment; this series simply did not test that.

What would make the result wrong? Selection toward lesions likely to do well, unmeasured depth of invasion (the paper states it was not determined), and team-assessed cosmesis could all inflate both control and cosmetic outcomes. What the paper does settle is feasibility: a mold could be made in three working days with two patient visits, sessions took 3 to 8 minutes, and no treatment was interrupted by applicator failure. For a radiation oncologist weighing how to treat a lesion on a curved facial surface, it supports surface-mold HDR as a geometrically sound option; the dose schedule to pair with it is a question this series leaves open.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: A custom PMMA mold held dose at 5 mm depth within 5% of prescription over curved facial anatomy with a sharp edge gradient, giving 99% 5y LC in primaries and no severe late effects at 180 cGy per fraction. It supports molds for non-flat sites; transfer to short-course schedules is untested.

open_questions: Does late cosmesis hold with hypofractionated HDR mold schedules?
Head-to-head vs superficial X-ray or electrons on curved facial sites
Durability of control beyond 5 years in recurrent lesions

studies.name: Fractionated HDR brachytherapy moulds for carcinoma of the pinna
studies.tldr: 13 pts with superficial pinna carcinoma treated with HDR moulds, 45 Gy/8 fx: complete resolution in all, no recurrences at minimum 18 mo f/u.
details: 🔍 Single-institution series (Christie Hospital), 13 pts treated up to July 1996

details.text: 🔍 Histology

details: 🔍 Lesions confined to pinna skin; dermal ultrasound confirmed no cartilage invasion in all but one

details.text: 💊 Single-plane moulds: 45 Gy surface dose in 8 fx over 5 days, HDR microselectron Ir stepping source

details: 🔍 Schedule: 1 fx Mon and Fri, 2 fx/day (≥6 h gap) on the three days between

details.text: 🔍 Mould height chosen so ultrasound-measured tumour depth sits inside the 80% isodose
📐 80% isodose falls at 1.5 to 3.5 mm depending on source height; gradient about 10% per mm
💊 One double-plane sandwich mould (full-thickness pinna, 10 mm plane separation): dose reduced to 42.5 Gy

details: 📊 Complete tumour resolution in all pts; no recurrences, no late RT complications at minimum 18 mo
📊 Acute reaction: moderate erythema confined to high-dose area, settled by first f/u visit at 6 wk
⚠️ No actuarial LC, no cosmesis scoring tool, no per-pt f/u reported
⚠️ Highly selected small cohort; authors state comparison with other modalities is difficult
⚠️ BED comparison table (Table 2) values cannot be tied to rows in extracted source

verdict.audience: Superficial BCC/SCC of the pinna, no cartilage invasion

studies.significance: The transferable parameter is ultrasound-guided mould height: measuring tumour depth (0.84 mm in one case) lets the 80% isodose cover disease while leaving cartilage outside, which electrons cannot do for lesions thinner than 12 mm. Full-thickness cases needed a sandwich mould at reduced dose (42.5 Gy), so cartilage sparing is the selection criterion.
studies.monday_clinic: In superficial BCC or SCC confined to pinna skin without cartilage invasion on ultrasound, this supports an HDR surface mould as a cartilage-sparing RT option; it does not address lesions requiring full-thickness pinna irradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective single-institution series of **13 pts** treated at the Christie Hospital up to July 1996. Technique description with three illustrative cases.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: 9 BCC, 3 SCC, 1 intraepidermal carcinoma. **Lesion confined to pinna skin**; dermal ultrasound confirmed **cartilage not invaded** in all but one.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: HDR microselectron with single stepping iridium source via custom vacuum-formed mould. **45 Gy in 8 fx over 5 days** prescribed to the surface, mould height set so tumour depth lies within the **80% isodose**. Sandwich mould case reduced to **42.5 Gy**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Complete tumour resolution in all pts**, barely perceptible scar. **No recurrences and no late complications** over minimum 18 mo f/u.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Moderate cutaneous erythema limited to the high-dose area, settled by the 6 wk visit. No discernible reaction on the contralateral pinna skin.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors position moulds against electrons (poor fall-off for thin lesions, cartilage necrosis risk), 30 kVp X-rays (dose inhomogeneity on curved surfaces, limited availability) and surgery (amputation or excision with graft). No head-to-head data.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents small superficial pinna carcinomas with intact cartilage on ultrasound. Does not represent cartilage-invading or deeply infiltrative lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Outcomes reported as a blanket statement without per-pt f/u, actuarial LC, or a validated cosmesis scale. Late cartilage toxicity can emerge beyond 18 mo, and the LQ-based BED rationale assumes complete repair between fractions.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The contribution is technique, not efficacy: ultrasound depth measurement plus tunable source height makes the plan conformal to sub-millimetre tumour thickness. Whether a higher late-tissue BED is tolerated because of the small volume is asserted, not shown.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a technique report with an outcome footnote rather than as efficacy evidence. Its real argument is physical. Thin cutaneous lesions on the pinna sit directly over avascular cartilage, and the modality chosen has to drop off steeply within a few millimetres. The authors make a coherent case that electrons cannot do this for small fields or thin lesions, that low-energy kilovoltage beams have become hard to source and dose evenly over a curved ear, and that a mould built at a chosen source-to-skin height lets the planner place the 80% isodose just beyond the measured tumour depth. Pairing this with transdermal ultrasound, validated against excised specimens in a separate small group, is what turns the mould from a historical Manchester-system device into a conformal tool.

The clinical outcome claims deserve much less weight. Thirteen selected pts, all with superficial disease and intact cartilage, is a population in which almost any competent local therapy would control the tumour. Complete resolution and no recurrence at a minimum of 18 months is reassuring but not discriminating, and the paper offers no per-patient follow-up distribution, no actuarial local control, and no structured cosmesis assessment. The excellent cosmesis is an investigator impression.

The fractionation choice is the part a modern reader should examine most carefully. Moving from low dose rate to HDR, the authors picked 45 Gy in 8 fractions, twice daily on the middle days, and justify it with an LQ comparison against familiar regimens. They concede the late-tissue BED is higher than conventional schedules and argue the tiny irradiated volume makes this acceptable. That is plausible, but late cartilage and skin effects are exactly the events an 18-month window is too short to capture. The one sandwich case, where full-thickness irradiation was unavoidable, received a reduced dose, which reflects the authors' own concern about cartilage tolerance.

What the paper changes is narrow: it supports offering a surface mould, or by extension a modern applicator approach with depth-guided prescription, to pts with superficial pinna BCC or SCC who are poor candidates for excision or graft. It does not settle durable control, late toxicity, or how the technique compares with surgery or electrons in matched pts. It would be wrong if late cartilage necrosis or deformity emerged after the reported window, or if the uniformly good outcomes reflected selection rather than technique.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable parameter is ultrasound-guided mould height: measuring tumour depth (0.84 mm in one case) lets the 80% isodose cover disease while leaving cartilage outside, which electrons cannot do for lesions thinner than 12 mm. Full-thickness cases needed a sandwich mould at reduced dose (42.5 Gy).

open_questions: Late cartilage toxicity beyond 18 months
Local control vs surgery or electrons in matched pts

With max skin dose ranging 125-150% and fractionation cut points spanning 2-5 cm, a reader building a skin HDR program has a variance map, not a constraint set.
studies.monday_clinic: For a BCC or cSCC on the pretibial skin, this survey supports treating site as a reason for gentler fractionation; it does not inform lesions deeper than 3 mm or with perineural invasion, which respondents steered away from brachytherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: 30-question electronic survey sent to ~400 **American Brachytherapy Society** clinician members. **16** fully completed surveys analyzed; one incomplete survey excluded. Nearly all US respondents, one from Spain.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Radiation oncologists using skin surface brachytherapy for **cSCC and BCC**. Practice settings spanned academic, hospital-based and private; aggregate experience ranged **8 to 1800 cases**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Hypofractionation preferred; clinical-scenario doses ranged **30 Gy in 5 fractions to 64 Gy in 32 fractions (EQD2 40 Gy-65 Gy)**. Median max prescription depth **5 mm**; shielded applicators most common, custom molds for large or curved areas. Respondents avoided daily schedules when hypofractionating.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Margin on gross disease **3-15mm, median 5mm**. Max skin dose **125-150% (median 135%)** of prescription; CTV coverage **90-100% (median 95%)**. **No consensus on dosimetric constraints**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Eight respondents described **severe acute and late toxicity on the lower extremity**, especially pretibial skin. Three referred non-healing in-field ulcers for hyperbaric oxygen.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The cited prior literature (Guix custom-mold HDR, Paravati electronic brachytherapy, van Hezewijk hypofractionated electrons) reports single-series outcomes. This survey adds no outcomes; it documents how widely dose, margin and constraints vary across practices using the technique.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents dosing and planning habits of ABS-member radiation oncologists treating BCC and cSCC with surface brachytherapy. Does not represent dermatology-delivered superficial RT, deep or perineural lesions, or measured clinical outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several key tables carry ambiguous row-value pairing in the source, and the scenario table (Table 4) was not captured. Toxicity is anecdotal recall with no denominators.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful output is the spread itself: margins, skin-dose ceilings and the lesion-size threshold for gentler fractionation all vary several-fold. Prospective trials and expert consensus are what the authors call for, and this survey cannot substitute for either.

studies.interpretation:
This paper is best read as a census of variation rather than evidence about the technique. Sixteen completed surveys from roughly 400 invitations is a small, self-selected sample, and the people who answer a voluntary ABS questionnaire about skin brachytherapy are plausibly those most invested in it. That selection cuts in a predictable direction: it likely overstates comfort with large fraction sizes and understates the frequency of abandonment after a bad outcome. The authors' conclusion that skin brachytherapy can be convenient and safe does not follow from the design, because no outcome was measured; safety here is the absence of reported catastrophe in recall, alongside eight respondents who did recall severe lower-extremity toxicity.

What the survey does establish is that there was no shared dosimetric language among users. Max skin dose ceilings of 125-150% of prescription, CTV coverage targets of 90-100%, and no respondent using D2cc, D1cc or D0.1cc means two programs can call the same plan acceptable or unacceptable. Some respondents planned only with applicator depth calculations, which is reasonable for flat shielded cones but leaves no common metric for comparing toxicity across centers. Any future outcomes series pooled across institutions inherits that heterogeneity.

Against the single-institution outcome series the authors cite, including custom-mold HDR for facial carcinomas and electronic brachytherapy reports, this survey sits one level lower in the evidence chain. Those series at least tie a schedule to a result. Here the dose range, 30 Gy in 5 fractions to 64 Gy in 32 fractions with EQD2 40 Gy-65 Gy, spans regimens that are not radiobiologically interchangeable for late skin effects, and the paper cannot say which end of that range buys better cosmesis or control.

The pretibial signal is the one finding with face validity for practice. Nearly unanimous de-escalation to 2-3 Gy per fraction on pretibial skin, plus the concentration of recalled severe toxicity there, matches the clinical intuition that poorly vascularized, edema-prone lower-leg skin tolerates large fractions badly. The non-healing ulcer case driven by post-treatment edema from systemic causes is a reminder that host factors, not just dose, determine the lower-extremity outcome.

The survey does not settle margin selection, the depth limit for surface brachytherapy beyond the respondents' 3 mm avoidance threshold, or whether brachytherapy's shorter course offsets any cosmetic cost relative to electrons or orthovoltage. Several respondents pointed to NCCN low- and high-risk definitions to set margins, which is the most portable takeaway: anchor margin decisions to histologic risk rather than to applicator convenience. For a program writing its own protocol, the value is knowing that the published practice range is wide enough that local constraints must be defined and audited internally.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable read is pretibial dosing: 10 respondents (63%) dropped to 2-3 Gy per fraction there, and eight reported severe lower-extremity toxicity. Max skin dose 125-150% and fractionation cut points of 2-5 cm mean a skin HDR program must set and audit its own constraints.

open_questions: Which dosimetric constraints predict late skin toxicity?
Optimal fractionation for pretibial and lower-extremity lesions
Brachytherapy vs electrons or orthovoltage for cosmesis

studies.name: CT-based flap brachytherapy for facial non-melanoma skin cancers
studies.tldr: 1-yr KM local control 92% after HDR flap brachy 40 Gy/8 fx twice weekly for T1 facial BCC/SCC; no chronic G≥3 toxicity.

details.text: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective review, 2007-2018; 50 pts, 53 lesions

details: 🔍 Pts selected mostly for inability to tolerate or refusal of surgery

details.text: 🔍 Population
subdetails: Histologically confirmed BCC 35 (66%) or SCC 18 (34%), AJCC 8th T1
Median tumor size 18 mm (5-20), thickness 5 mm (3-7)
Area H 40 (75%), nose most common site 17 (32%)

details.text: 💊 RT technique
subdetails: 40 Gy/8 fx twice weekly (BED 60 Gy, α/β 10), Ir-192 HDR
CTV = visible tumor + 5 mm, no PTV margin
Catheter flap: channels 5 mm from surface, 10 mm apart; thermoplastic mask fixation
5 mm intranasal / under-eyelid / gingivolabial spacer for OAR sparing

details.text: 📊 1-yr KM local control 92%; 4 local recurrences (2 nasal SCC, 1 eyelid BCC, 1 lip BCC)
📊 Good/excellent cosmesis with complete remission in 49 lesions (92%)
📊 Toxicity

details: 📊 All 8 eyelid/periorbital pts developed G1 conjunctivitis, resolved with 2-day antibiotic/steroid drops

details.text: ⚠️ Median f/u 15 mo (range 6-27): too short for BCC late recurrence or late skin effects
⚠️ Median V100 85% sits below the stated goal of ≥95% PTV coverage

details: ⚠️ Internal inconsistencies: abstract calls the 3 acute events G2, Results G3; Discussion claims no chronic G≥2 despite 2 G2 telangiectasias

details.text: 🔗 Within the 87%-100% LC range of prior retrospective HDR surface-mold series cited by the authors

verdict.rationale: Single-arm retrospective series, surgery-unfit/refusing pts, 15-mo median f/u; no comparator vs Mohs or EBRT. Consistent with prior HDR surface-mold series.
verdict.audience: T1 facial BCC/SCC (area H/M), elderly, surgery-unfit or refusing

studies.significance: The dosimetry is the transferable part: median V100 85% and D90 92% with catheters 5 mm off the skin, against tumors up to 7 mm thick, so deep-margin coverage is the weak point. Three of 4 recurrences were nose, eyelid and lip, the irregular sites the flap is meant to solve.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with T1 BCC or SCC of the nose, eyelid or temple who declines or cannot tolerate Mohs, this supports CT-planned flap HDR 40 Gy/8 fx as a reasonable option; it does not address pts fit for surgery or lesions thicker than 7 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective** review, January 2007 to December 2018. **50 pts, 53 lesions**, minimum 6 mo follow-up, median follow-up **15 mo** (range 6-27). LC by Kaplan-Meier.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Histologically confirmed **BCC or SCC, AJCC 8th T1**, all NCCN high-risk by area H or area M location. Median age 80; selected by a multidisciplinary dermatology clinic, mostly for **inability to tolerate or refusal of surgery**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **40 Gy in 8 fractions twice weekly** (BED 60 Gy, α/β 10) via Ir-192 HDR catheter flap, CT-planned in BrachyVision. **CTV = visible tumor + 5 mm**, PTV = CTV with no margin; 5 mm spacers protected the nasal mucosa, globe and gingiva.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **1-yr LC 92%**, 4 local recurrences, 3 in nose/eyelid/lip. **49 lesions (92%)** had good/excellent cosmesis with complete remission.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute G1 60%, G2 35%, G3 5%, all after fraction 5. Chronic G2 telangiectasia in **2 pts (4%)** at 12 mo, **no chronic G≥3**, no toxicity-related hospitalization.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Local control falls inside the **87%-100%** range of prior retrospective HDR surface-mold series. The only randomized surgery-vs-RT trial in facial BCC cited by the authors found 4-yr failure **7.5% vs 0.7%** favoring surgery, though RT there was mostly interstitial brachy, not surface HDR.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly pts with T1 facial BCC/SCC ≤7 mm thick who are poor surgical candidates or decline surgery. Does not represent surgery-fit pts, deeply infiltrating or T2+ tumors, or perineural disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Median V100 85% falls short of the ≥95% PTV coverage goal, and depth was assessed mostly by palpation. Abstract and body disagree on acute toxicity grade, and the Discussion understates chronic G2 events.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The flap's value is conformity on irregular surfaces where surface molds and electrons struggle, yet recurrences clustered in exactly those sites. BCC and SCC got identical dose and margins, consistent with NCCN, the 2020 ASTRO guideline and the 2019 ABS consensus, so histology-specific dosing is still untested.

studies.interpretation:
This series belongs to a familiar genre: a single-institution, retrospective account of a brachytherapy technique applied to elderly pts who either could not tolerate or would not accept Mohs surgery. Its 1-yr local control of 92% sits comfortably inside the 87% to 100% range the authors cite from earlier HDR surface-mold series, so the result is best read as a technical confirmation that a CT-planned catheter flap performs like other surface applicators, not as evidence that it performs better. The comparison that actually defines the field is the randomized trial of surgery vs RT in facial BCC that the authors themselves cite, where 4-yr failure was 7.5% with RT vs 0.7% with surgery. Nothing here challenges that ordering for a pt who can have surgery, and the authors do not claim it does.

The more instructive content is dosimetric. The flap places its source channels 5 mm from the skin, the CTV adds a 5 mm margin with no PTV expansion, and median tumor thickness was 5 mm with a range up to 7 mm. Against that geometry, the median V100 of 85% and D90 of 92% mean that a typical plan left part of the target below prescription, despite a stated goal of covering at least 95% of the PTV. Depth was assessed largely by palpation, with pathologic depth used only when available. For a reader deciding whether to adopt a flap technique, the open issue is the deep margin of thicker lesions, and this series cannot resolve it because recurrences were few and follow-up short.

The pattern of failure is worth more than its four events suggest. Two nasal SCCs, an eyelid BCC and a lip BCC recurred, all in the irregular, high-curvature anatomy the flap is meant to handle better than a rigid mold or an electron field. That is not proof of a technique-specific weakness, since these are also the highest-risk sites in any series, but it argues against assuming the flap has solved conformity on the nose and lip.

Follow-up is the decisive limitation for interpreting both efficacy and toxicity. A median of 15 months, with some lesions observed for only 6, is short for BCC, whose recurrences can declare late, and short for late skin effects after a hypofractionated schedule. The authors lean on Gauden et al., with 66-month median follow-up, to argue that chronic toxicity stabilizes in the first one to two years, which is plausible but borrowed rather than shown. The toxicity reporting also contains internal inconsistencies: the abstract lists the three acute events as grade 2 while the results call them grade 3, and the discussion states there were no chronic grade 2 or higher toxicities while the results report two pts with grade 2 telangiectasia at 12 months. Neither changes the overall picture of a tolerable schedule, but both lower confidence in the precision of the toxicity numbers.

What would make this wrong is a late recurrence curve that diverges from the 1-yr estimate, or deep-margin failures in thicker tumors once larger numbers accumulate. The decision it supports is narrow: for a surgery-unfit pt with a thin T1 facial lesion, 40 Gy in 8 twice-weekly HDR fractions via a flap is a reasonable, convenient option with acceptable acute effects. Whether BCC and SCC should receive different dose or margins, and how surface HDR compares with EBRT or Mohs head to head, remain open.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The dosimetry is the transferable part: median V100 85% and D90 92% with catheters 5 mm off the skin, against tumors up to 7 mm thick, so deep-margin coverage is the weak point. Three of 4 recurrences were nose, eyelid and lip, the irregular sites the flap is meant to solve.

open_questions: Durability of local control and late cosmesis beyond 2 years
Histology-specific dose or margin for BCC vs SCC
Surface HDR brachytherapy vs Mohs or EBRT head to head

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective review of all Ir-192 HDR surface mould cases at one BC Cancer center, **2010-2017**, **65 lesions in 59 pts**. Median follow-up **8 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Median age **82** (45-97). **BCC 54%**, **SCC 31%**, plus melanoma, lentigo maligna, Merkel cell, cutaneous NHL and one keloid. Mostly head and neck (forehead/temple, nose, scalp, cheek/lip); **7 lesions palliative-intent**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Individualized Aquaplast + superflab mould, catheters ~1 cm apart, CT-based planning in BrachyVision. Most common **40 Gy/10 fx** (48.2%); range 15 Gy/3 to 60 Gy/30 fx. Prescribed at **0.5 cm depth**, CTV from clinical wire with **no PTV expansion**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **2-yr LC 84.9%**, 2-yr PFS 71.5%, 2-yr OS 77.6%; **CR 96.8%** at 2-4 mo. Of 20 deaths, only two were from the skin malignancy. No dosimetric or histologic factor reached significance on univariate analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No G3-5 acute or late toxicity.** Acute G2 dermatitis 32% and ulceration 8%; one late G2 necrosis (2%) appearing around 10 months.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors place their LC within the brachytherapy literature range of 83.3% to 100% and against EBRT LC of 87-100% and Mohs at 95-99%. Gauden et al. reported LC 98% with 36 Gy/12 fx, but at similarly short follow-up and largely in a post-resection margin-positive setting. GEC-ESTRO grades the technique B.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly, often comorbid pts with superficial head-and-neck skin cancers for whom surgery is not suitable. Does not represent lesions deeper than 5 mm or younger pts fit for Mohs.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Histology and intent are pooled (keloid, lymphoma, melanoma, palliative lesions). Toxicity was graded retrospectively from records and photographs, and cosmesis was not scored. Internal inconsistencies (median age 82 vs 83, follow-up 8 vs 9 mo, sex counts summing to 65 of 59 pts) lower confidence in the tabulated data.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The series shows the technique is deliverable and tolerable in a very old cohort, which is the realistic use case. It does not settle the durability of control, the right prescription depth or margin, or whether coverage metrics predict recurrence.

studies.interpretation:
This series does what most single-center skin brachytherapy reports do. It shows that a CT-planned, custom mould HDR approach can be delivered to a very old, comorbid population without grade 3 toxicity, and that early response is near universal. What it cannot show is long-term local control. The headline 2-yr LC of 84.9% is an actuarial projection from a cohort followed for a median of 8 months, in which a third of pts died, mostly of unrelated causes. With that much censoring, the 2-yr figure should be read as a statement about the first year rather than a durable control estimate, and the late toxicity profile, including the single grade 2 necrosis appearing around month 10, is almost certainly incomplete.

Against the comparators the authors cite, the result is plausible but not reassuring on its own terms. They frame their LC as consistent with brachytherapy reports ranging from 83.3% to 100% and EBRT reports of 87-100%, while Mohs sits at 95-99%. Their figure falls at the bottom of each range. The Gauden series they lean on reported LC 98% with 36 Gy/12 fx, but at a comparably short follow-up and in a setting dominated by post-resection margin-positive disease, which is a more favorable target than gross tumor in an elderly pt. Cross-series comparison here is weak in both directions, and the authors acknowledge that this literature is small and retrospective, which is why GEC-ESTRO grades the technique B.

The more useful content for a planning radiation oncologist is the dosimetry. Prescribing at 0.5 cm with no PTV margin and a 90% coverage intent produced a median V100 of 73.7% and V90 of 92.3%, with a surface dose of 126.5%. The univariate split, LC 88.9% when V90 exceeded 95% vs 76.9% below, points in the direction one would expect, and the same is true for median target dose above vs below 100%. None of these reached significance, and with five local recurrences the analysis had essentially no power, so the right reading is that coverage may matter and this dataset cannot tell how much. Whether a modest CTV-to-PTV margin, which the authors note is controversial in brachytherapy, would close that gap is the practical question the data raise.

The histology split cuts against expectation: BCC LC 70% vs SCC 88.2%, with three of the five recurrences being nasal BCC. That is more likely a small-numbers artifact or a reflection of nasal geometry and mould conformity than a biologic signal, but it is a reason not to assume BCC is the easy case for this technique on the nose.

The decision this informs is narrow. For a frail pt with a superficial head-and-neck BCC or SCC who is not a Mohs candidate, surface mould HDR is a tolerable, non-invasive option with high early response. It does not establish equivalence with surgery or EBRT, and it says nothing about lesions deeper than 5 mm. Pooled histologies, mixed intent and visible internal inconsistencies in the reported demographics and follow-up should temper how much weight any single number carries.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Prescription at 0.5 cm with no PTV gave median V100 73.7% and surface dose 126.5%. LC 88.9% with V90 >95% vs 76.9% below (p=0.85) suggests coverage matters, but five recurrences cannot define a V90 target or justify a margin.

open_questions: Durability of local control beyond one year of follow-up
Does V90 coverage above 95% predict local control?
Role of a PTV margin in surface mould brachytherapy

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomised phase II**, 1:1 by minimisation, stratified by histology, N-stage, met number, brain mets, SACT and site. **N=200** registered, **N=134** randomised; follow-up for 3 years or until death.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **De novo synchronous oligometastatic NSCLC without driver mutation**: 1-5 mets in up to 3 organs, PS 0-1, PET-CT and brain CT/MRI staged. Brain mets allowed only with at least one extracranial met. Randomised only with **CR/PR/SD and PS 0-2 after 6-8 weeks induction SACT**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Conventional RT or SABR to the primary (+/- nodes) plus **SABR/SRS to all metastases**, delivered within a window of up to 4-6 further weeks of induction SACT. Dose and fractionation not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: PFS, OS, QoL and AEs reported. Which endpoint was primary is not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: PFS improved with RT (no effect size in source). OS **HR 0.99 (95% CI 0.63-1.55), p=0.95**; mOS 31.0 vs 28.0 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No significant difference in AEs or QoL** per presenter; no rates in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Gomez (Lancet Oncol 2016) and Iyengar (JAMA Oncol 2018) supported LCT after chemotherapy, while Elamin (ESMO 2025) and Iyengar (ASCO 2024) found no LCT benefit in oligo-persistent disease on chemo-IO. SARON's **OS-null** result sits with the latter.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents de novo synchronous oligometastatic driver-negative NSCLC without progression after induction SACT. Does not represent EGFR-mutated disease on TKI, progressors on induction, or pts with more than 5 mets or 3 organs.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The schema lists 134 randomised but the OS at-risk table shows 70 per arm, unresolved in source. Maintenance SACT was permitted, and its use by arm is not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Comprehensive RT bought PFS without measured toxicity or QoL cost, but **no OS benefit** at this sample size. The CI is wide enough that a moderate OS effect in either direction is not excluded.

studies.interpretation:
SARON lands in a literature that has been drifting away from the early optimism about local consolidative therapy in oligometastatic NSCLC. The trial's own background slide lays out the arc: Gomez (Lancet Oncol 2016) and Iyengar (JAMA Oncol 2018) supported consolidation after chemotherapy, the EGFR-mutated TKI trials (Wang, JNCI 2023; Sun, JCO 2024) extended that to targeted therapy, and the more recent chemo-immunotherapy era data (Iyengar, ASCO 2024; Elamin, ESMO 2025) found no benefit in oligo-persistent disease. SARON asks the cleanest version of the question for the largest group, de novo synchronous driver-negative disease, and its answer on survival is null: HR 0.99 with mOS 31.0 vs 28.0 months.

The PFS-positive, OS-null pattern is familiar and has two readings. One is that consolidation RT delays progression at sites a subsequent line would have controlled anyway, so it moves the timing of failure without changing its endpoint. The other is that SARON could not see an OS effect that exists. The confidence interval, 0.63 to 1.55, cannot exclude a meaningful benefit or meaningful harm, and that width is what a randomised phase II produces for survival. The honest summary is that OS is undetermined rather than disproven, while the absence of any signal at all should temper expectations.

The design choices matter for how far the result travels. Randomisation happened after 6 to 8 weeks of induction SACT and only for pts with CR, PR or SD, so the trial tests consolidation in a population already selected for systemic sensitivity. That is the right population for the clinical question most radiation oncologists face, but it says nothing about upfront local therapy or about pts who progress on induction. Maintenance SACT was allowed, and without per-arm data on maintenance use and subsequent lines, the OS comparison is exposed to post-progression treatment differences. The source also leaves a numerical inconsistency: the schema lists 134 randomised, while the OS at-risk table starts at 70 per arm. That needs to be resolved in the full report before the numbers are cited.

What the trial does seem to establish is that comprehensive RT to the primary and all metastases did not cost QoL or add measurable toxicity, according to the presenter. That reframes the decision. Consolidation RT in this setting becomes a disease-control intervention with an apparently acceptable cost, reasonable to discuss when local progression would itself be morbid, rather than a survival intervention to offer every eligible pt. Two things would change the read: a PFS magnitude large enough to matter clinically, which the source does not give, and longer follow-up or pooled data showing late OS separation. Until the full PFS data and the endpoint are reported, the trial is better taken as evidence against a large OS effect than as a settled verdict on consolidation.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Comprehensive RT (primary +/- nodes by conventional RT or SABR, plus SABR/SRS to all mets) improved PFS without a QoL or AE penalty but left OS unchanged (HR 0.99). Consolidation for non-progressors after induction is a disease-control decision, not a survival one.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: In pts who respond or stabilise on induction SACT, adding RT did not change OS (mOS 31.0 vs 28.0 mo). The systemic backbone and maintenance remain the survival lever, and per-arm subsequent therapy is not reported in source.

open_questions: Does the PFS gain translate to OS with longer follow-up?
Role of consolidation RT on a chemo-immunotherapy backbone
Which oligometastatic subsets benefit (met number, brain mets)?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Pooled cohort from four neoadjuvant/perioperative trials (PURE-01, SURE-01, SURE-02, NURE-Combo), **N=279** enrolled 02/2017-07/2025. Bladder preservation was pt choice, not a randomized allocation.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **MIBC cT2-4N0M0**, pure/predominant (≥50%) urothelial carcinoma. The reTURBT group (**n=54**) declined RC and required **negative imaging, biopsy and cytology**.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Pembrolizumab, sacituzumab govitecan, SG + pembrolizumab, or nivolumab + nab-paclitaxel, restaged with CT + multiparametric bladder MRI. Adjuvant/maintenance per protocol; **deferred RC or chemo-RT only for residual tumor or recurrence**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Whole reTURBT group: **36-mo EFS 66.7%**, **36-mo OS 82.7%**; 19% recurred, 13% distantly. Outcomes split sharply by response at reTURBT (Fig 2).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The comparator is the trials' own RC cohort, not a randomized arm. Trimodality therapy, the established bladder-sparing alternative, was not a planned arm here; chemo-RT appears only as salvage.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents MIBC pts with ypT0 at reTURBT after neoadjuvant IO- or ADC-based therapy who decline RC. Does not represent pts with residual disease at reTURBT, node-positive disease, or non-urothelial-predominant histology.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Four different regimens pooled into one small cohort. The tweet's comparison claim is truncated, and the **30/54 (56%) vs 43/213 (20%)** schema figure carries no endpoint label in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The pCR stratum looks good, but HRs vs RC of **1.96 (0.53-7.27)** for EFS and **0.90 (0.10-8.40)** for OS are too imprecise to call equivalence. Non-pCR at reTURBT is the clear failure mode and argues for definitive local therapy rather than continued surveillance.

studies.interpretation:
The question this cohort asks is narrower than it first looks. It does not test bladder preservation as a strategy against cystectomy. It describes what happened to the fifth of trial pts who, after neoadjuvant or perioperative systemic therapy, chose not to have their bladder removed and were restaged with reTURBT, MRI and cytology. That choice is the central methodological fact. Pts who decline RC differ from those who accept it in ways no restaging protocol captures: comorbidity, preference, perhaps a clinician's read of an exceptional response. Every comparison with the RC cohort inherits that selection, and the direction of the bias is hard to predict.

Within that frame, the useful signal is the split by response at reTURBT rather than the pooled numbers. Pts with no residual disease had 24-mo EFS 87.6% and OS 96.7%, and their HRs against RC pCR pts were 1.96 for EFS and 0.90 for OS, with intervals from 0.53 to 7.27 and 0.10 to 8.40. Those intervals are wide enough to fit real harm or real equivalence. The point estimate for EFS leans toward more events without the bladder out, which is expected: an intact bladder can grow new urothelial tumors, and some of those events are salvageable. A reader should not take the OS estimate as evidence of no survival cost. At this sample size it cannot exclude one.

The non-pCR stratum is more decisive. Residual disease at reTURBT went with 24-mo EFS 19.3% and OS 50.4%, against 67.8% and 82.5% for non-pCR pts who had RC. Even allowing for selection, that gap is large enough to treat residual disease at reTURBT as a firm stop signal for surveillance. For a radiation oncologist, this is where the cohort touches practice: chemo-RT was used here only as salvage for residual tumor or recurrence, never as planned consolidation. Whether planned chemoradiation after an incomplete response to modern IO- or ADC-based neoadjuvant therapy would close that gap is untested here, and it is the more interesting trial.

Trimodality therapy remains the bladder-sparing approach with the longer evidence base, and this cohort does not compete with it directly; it proposes a route that omits RT altogether for the best responders. That is plausible biologically, but four different regimens are pooled, follow-up runs only to 36 mo, and the reported recurrence rate of 19% includes 13% distant. For the result to be wrong in the direction that matters, late bladder recurrences after 36 mo would need to convert to metastatic disease at rates the current follow-up cannot see. Prospective selection criteria, ideally with a molecular marker added to imaging and cytology, are what would turn this from a description of self-selected responders into a usable pathway.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Chemo-RT was used only as salvage for residual tumor or recurrence, so this tests bladder sparing without upfront RT. Non-pCR at reTURBT gave 24-mo OS 50.4% vs 82.5% after RC, marking residual disease as the point where definitive local therapy, including chemoRT, belongs.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Response at reTURBT after pembrolizumab-, SG- or nivolumab-based neoadjuvant therapy separated outcomes sharply: 24-mo EFS 87.6% with ypT0 vs 19.3% with residual disease. Depth of response to the systemic regimen, not the regimen label, drove eligibility for surveillance.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: ypT0 at reTURBT pts who declined RC had 24-mo OS 96.7%, but EFS HR 1.96 (0.53-7.27) vs RC pCR is too imprecise to call equivalence. Residual disease at reTURBT tracked with far worse outcomes than RC, keeping cystectomy the default for incomplete responders.

Would planned chemoRT rescue non-pCR pts at reTURBT?
Can ctDNA or MRI better select pts for surveillance?
